Wall Street posts its best week since August despite Nvidia's slide, but US yields jump and the dollar nears a 19-month high

On Friday, November 13, the S&P 500 fell 0.4% and the Nasdaq 0.9%, dragged down by chipmakers, but the S&P 500 ended the week up 2.5%. Meanwhile, US interest rates saw their sharpest rise in more than two years, and the dollar soared [1][2][3][9].
On Friday, the S&P 500 lost 31 points (-0.40%) to 7,561.67, and the Nasdaq 230 points (-0.91%) to 25,136.27; the Dow Jones ended slightly higher, up about 0.1%, at around 52,350 points [1][2].
Over the week, the S&P 500 gained 2.5%, its first positive week since October and its best since August; the Nasdaq posted its first weekly gain in five weeks [1][2].

Chipmakers weighed on the market: Nvidia fell about 2%, Broadcom 4.8% and AMD 8.75% [2][5]. Nvidia lost more than $600 billion in value over the week and has now fallen for six straight weeks, a first since 2012 [2][4].
October producer prices rose 0.3% month on month, slightly less than the expected 0.4%, but 6.5% year on year, the biggest increase since November 2022 [6][7].

In bonds, the 2-year yield, which is highly sensitive to Federal Reserve (Fed) decisions, was heading for its biggest weekly rise in more than two years, peaking at 4.892% [9]. The 10-year yield reached about 5.16% on Friday, its highest since October [10].
The dollar had its best week since September, near a 19-month high, lifted by bets on a rate hike in December; Fed Governor Christopher Waller said he would not rule out a half-point hike [8].
US crude fell 0.34% to $88.44, and Brent ended at $95.70 [11]. Bitcoin dropped below $70,000, its lowest since August [12].

Key takeaway: the US stock market held up thanks to companies outside tech, while two forces are working against it: the leadership crisis at Nvidia, a pillar of artificial intelligence (AI), and a Fed that seems ready to raise rates to curb inflation [2][4][8].

The mechanism works through interest rates: when inflation proves stubborn (6.5% year on year for producer prices), markets expect a hike in the policy rate. Bond yields rise, which makes stocks less attractive, especially those of growth companies such as chipmakers [6][9][10].
Higher rates also draw capital into the dollar, at the expense of the euro, emerging-market currencies and speculative investments such as bitcoin [8][12].
Next week will be a test for AI: Nvidia reports earnings on Tuesday, November 17, without Jensen Huang, and Anthropic lists on the Nasdaq on November 19 [13][14].

For you, the effect comes first through the dollar: the higher it rises, the more oil, which is paid for in dollars, and trips to the United States cost in euros. Rising US rates also push up European rates, and therefore the cost of loans over time. No buy or sell advice here.

Netherlands: seven hours of crisis talks to save the Jetten government after a “millionaires' tax” passed without the liberal right

Rob Jetten's Dutch government came close to collapse: on Thursday evening, two coalition parties passed a tax package with the left, against the VVD, their liberal right-wing partner. After seven hours of crisis talks on Friday, November 13, the VVD is staying, but wants to renegotiate [1][2][3].

On the evening of Thursday, November 12, lawmakers from D66, the Prime Minister's party, and the CDA (Christian Democrats) backed amendments from two opposition parties, PRO and Volt, to pass the tax package by a narrow majority [1][2]. VVD lawmakers voted against it [2].

PRO leader Jesse Klaver calls one of the measures a “millionaires' tax”: a new levy on income from savings and assets [1]. According to the Dutch press, it would raise the bill for the wealthiest by €1 billion a year [5]. Its supporters say it funds tax cuts for low earners [1].

VVD leader Dilan Yeşilgöz-Zegerius, who is also defense minister, says she was caught off guard and considers the deal contrary to the coalition agreement [1]. Her party argues that taxing wealth more heavily will push entrepreneurs to leave the country [5].

On Friday, Rob Jetten met for about seven hours with Dilan Yeşilgöz and CDA leader Bart van den Brink [3][4]. According to the ANP news agency, NOS, RTL and De Telegraaf, the VVD is staying in the coalition, at least for now [3].
“Nobody expects endless political squabbling in The Hague or new elections,” Rob Jetten argued [1]. He acknowledges a “unique” situation and believes the coalition needs “a lot of improvement” [3].

The VVD is demanding a “substantive correction” and a different “political balance,” according to De Telegraaf; according to the daily AD, it could seek to bring another right-wing party into the coalition [3]. Further talks are planned in the coming days [2].

Deputy Prime Minister Van den Brink points out that the VVD also gains a lot, such as the reform of wealth taxation known as “box 3” [6]. The package still has to pass the Dutch Senate, where its fate is uncertain [5].
Key takeaway: the Netherlands has a minority government hanging by a thread, with only 66 of 150 seats in the House, less than nine months after taking office [1][7].

At heart, the conflict is economic: who should pay? On one side, the center and the left want to tax large fortunes to ease the burden on low incomes; on the other, the liberal right fears an exodus of entrepreneurs and capital [1][5].

The Dutch case adds to a series of budget crises in Europe: Spain votes on November 29 after Parliament was dissolved, and the Belgian government tendered its resignation in early November after budget talks failed [7].

The Netherlands is a key country in European budget debates: the fall of the government in The Hague would slow down EU decisions, particularly on funding for Ukraine. And the debate over taxing large fortunes resembles the one around France's 2027 budget.

news.2026-11-14-cuba-trump-force-militai: Cuba: Trump wants to “finish” the regime before 2029 and does not rule out military action; Havana says it is ready to defend itself

In an interview aired on November 12, Donald Trump said he wants to settle the Cuban question before leaving the White House in 2029 and would “certainly” consider a short military operation. Cuba, cut off from oil by the US blockade, replies that its future “will never be decided in the north” [1][2][4].

On Thursday, November 12, speaking to conservative host Hugh Hewitt, Donald Trump said he wants to “get Cuba done” before the end of his term in 2029, and that he “would certainly consider” a short military operation [1][3].

He cited his Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents are Cuban, who “would love to do it” [1][3]. The previous Monday, he had predicted that the Cuban government “would fall pretty quickly” [2].
Trump says Washington is “talking” with Cuba, without saying with whom or about what; Cuban officials have not described any negotiations [2].

Since February 2026, the United States has been blocking tankers heading to Cuba and targeting companies that deliver fuel there [2]. For months, the island has suffered nationwide power outages and shortages of fuel and food [1][2].

On November 10, President Miguel Díaz-Canel wrote on X that “the future of Cuba will never be decided in the north,” invoking the 1959 revolution [4][5]. He said he was “determined to repel any attempt at foreign military aggression,” noting that Cuba does not threaten US security [2].

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla accuses Washington of seeking to cause a “humanitarian catastrophe” with its fuel restrictions [2]. Marco Rubio, for his part, told the G7 foreign ministers' meeting in France that the “end goal” was a better future for Cuba [5].
As early as January, the Wall Street Journal reported meetings in Miami and Washington with Cuban exiles and civic groups, aimed at finding a regime official willing to “cut a deal” [6].
Key takeaway: this is the first time Trump has spoken so clearly about using force against Cuba, following the operation that led to the capture of Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela this year [1][7].

The US strategy is primarily economic: by cutting off fuel deliveries, Washington deprives the island of the energy its power plants need, hence the massive blackouts [2]. Havana denounces “collective punishment” and says the threat is not Cuba but the blockade [4].

Trump and Rubio, who is in charge of the file, keep up the ambiguity between negotiation and threat: in early November, in front of conservatives gathered at Mar-a-Lago, the president even joked about “parachuting” Rubio into Cuba [2]. He also says the United States is already providing humanitarian aid to the island [2].

No direct effect on your daily life. But a US intervention in the Caribbean, after Venezuela, would open a new geopolitical front while the United States is already at war with Iran, and would raise tensions with Havana's allies. It could also trigger a new wave of Cubans leaving the island, a migration issue that also affects Spain and the European Union.

Venezuela: $15.6 billion in oil revenue collected since Maduro's fall, almost all of it going to salaries and pensions

Delcy Rodríguez's interim government published its accounts on November 12: $15.6 billion in oil and mining revenue from January to November, of which $14.7 billion was paid to public employees and retirees. Washington, which keeps the money in an account under its supervision, published its own report the same day [1][2][3].

According to the report presented on Thursday, November 12, Venezuela collected $15.603 billion between January and November 2026, of which $15.148 billion, or 97.1%, came from sales of oil and oil products [2][3].
Spending reached $14.86 billion: $14.71 billion for public sector salaries and pensions, $150.5 million for running the state; a balance of $742.9 million remains [2][3].
Interim President Delcy Rodríguez says that “99 dollars out of 100” went to salaries and pensions: this is true of spending, but it represents 94.3% of revenue [2][4].

The money goes through an account held in US custody: Venezuela's central bank must request the release of funds and justify how they are used [3]. The government refers to its “Transparencia Soberana” portal for details [3].

The State Department published a report the same day covering the period from January 3 to September 30: $12.264 billion deposited into this “Venezuela custody account,” $12.108 billion disbursed and a balance of $168.6 million [1][4].

The opposition disputes this: the Primero Justicia party says “not a single dollar” has been invested in the country and points out that the legal minimum wage has been frozen at 130 bolívars a month since March 2022, less than one dollar [5][6].
In July, Donald Trump said the United States had already sold more than $13 billion worth of Venezuelan oil since the capture of Nicolás Maduro [7].

Key takeaway: since Maduro's fall, Venezuela's oil revenue has flowed through Washington, which collects, holds and releases the money. The two reports published on the same day offer a rare overview of this unprecedented system [1][3].

The figures show how fragile the country is: almost all of the revenue goes to paying for the day-to-day running of the state, and almost nothing goes to investment, which the opposition denounces [2][5].

The system is also debated in the United States: back in April, Democratic lawmaker Joaquin Castro asked the US Government Accountability Office (GAO) to audit the fund [8]. US control over Venezuelan money remains one of Washington's main levers over Caracas [3].

Venezuelan oil resold under US control adds supply to the global market at a time when the war with Iran is pushing prices up: it provides a small cushion for the price of a barrel, and therefore for filling up your tank or your heating oil bill.

European stocks: the Stoxx 600 notches a third record and its best week since June; the CAC 40 ends a “perfect week” up 2.8%

On Friday, November 13, the pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed at 664.14 points, a third straight record close, and gained about 2.4% over the week. Insurers and oil companies offset the slump in chip stocks Infineon and ASML, dragged down by the crisis at Nvidia [1][2][3].

The Stoxx 600 rose 0.02% to 664.14 points, its third record close in a row, and posted its best week since June [2][3]. The Euro Stoxx 50, which groups the 50 largest companies in the eurozone, fell 0.19% to 6,386.86 [2].

In Paris, the CAC 40 closed at 8,368.91 points (+0.09%), its highest level since late August, according to AFP [4]. It rose on all five days of the week and gained 2.8%, according to BFM Bourse [5][6].
In Frankfurt, the DAX slipped 0.08% to 26,749.95 points, weighed down by Infineon; in London, the FTSE 100 gained 0.36% to 10,902.56 points [7].
Chipmakers tumbled: Infineon lost 4.3% and ASML 2.8%, following US artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, which are worried about the leadership change at Nvidia [2].
Insurers held up the market: Allianz and Munich Re each gained about 1%, after better-than-expected results published on Thursday, and AXA rose 1.1% [2].
These gains came despite Goldman Sachs, which downgraded European insurers to “underweight” for 2027, meaning it advises clients to hold less of them than their weight in the index [2].
The Paris session was also disrupted by a global outage of Microsoft's online services, including Outlook, according to BFM Bourse [5].

Key takeaway: Europe benefits from a stock market that is less dependent on AI than Wall Street. Its main indices are weighted mostly toward banks, insurers, luxury and energy, which suffer less when chips fall [1][2].

Insurers are among the few winners from rising rates: they invest their customers' premiums in bonds, and every extra point of yield increases their investment income. That is why they hold firm when rates rise [1][2].

The risk comes from chips: Infineon and ASML are Europe's two main gateways into AI, and they are following Nvidia down. On November 5, Infineon had already lost more than 8% in a single session [2][8].
The record remains fragile: it rests on one week of good corporate results, while bond yields are also rising in Europe, which is holding back gains [1][3].

For you, these records affect your savings if you have a French equity savings plan (PEA), unit-linked life insurance or a European index fund: their value tracks the CAC 40 and the Stoxx 600. A record says nothing about what comes next, and a week of gains can quickly be wiped out. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why an index can hit a record while tech falls

An index like the Stoxx 600 is a weighted average of 600 companies: each one counts according to its market value. If chipmakers fall but insurers, banks and oil companies rise, the index can still go up, as it did on Friday [2]. This is called a rotation: money leaves a sector seen as too expensive or too risky and moves into others. Insurers benefit when rates rise, because they invest their customers' money in bonds, which then pay more [1][2]. On Wall Street, tech giants carry much more weight in the indices: their fall drags the whole market down, even when more than 60% of stocks are rising [10].
Precedents: when tech shakes the indices
March 10, 2000
The Nasdaq, the index of US technology stocks, reaches 5,132.52 points at the peak of the dot-com bubble [11].
It did not set a new record until April 2015, fifteen years later [11].
The Nasdaq loses 33.1% over the year, its worst year since 2008, as the Fed raises rates to fight inflation [12].
Rising rates hit growth stocks first, since their value rests on distant profits [12].
November 5, 2026
Infineon loses 8.63% and Rheinmetall 16.46%; the DAX gives up an intraday record of 26,693 points and closes down 0.4% [8].
Five days later, a raised forecast is enough to make Infineon rebound: AI-related stocks remain highly volatile [13].

Brazil: the dollar ends at 5.65 reais, its highest of the year, as markets judge Lula's savings plan passed by the Senate too timid

On Friday, November 13, the dollar closed at about 5.65 reais, its highest close of 2026 and since June 2025, after rising more than 2.6% over the week. Investors find the 60 billion reais savings plan, adopted at first reading in the Senate, insufficient [1][2][3][4].

The dollar ended slightly higher, at 5.65 reais according to Metrópoles and 5.655 according to Cruzeiro FM: its highest close of 2026 and the highest since June 2, 2025, when it closed at 5.673 [1][2].
Over the week, the US currency gained 2.63% against the real, according to BPMoney [3].

On Thursday, the Senate approved the base text of bill PLP 299/2026 by 45 votes to 31; four disputed points are to be voted on Tuesday, November 17, before the bill goes to the Chamber of Deputies [5].
According to Planning Minister Bruno Moretti, the measures could save up to 60 billion reais ($10.75 billion) in 2027, or about 0.5% of gross domestic product (GDP) [4].

Armando Armenta of asset manager AllianceBernstein believes the effort needed is larger than this proposal for 2027; Maria Carolina Luchesi of Hike Capital says markets want lasting limits on spending [4].
The stock market held up better: the Ibovespa gained 0.66% to 172,457.76 points, and 2.35% over the week [2][6].
The real is also facing headwinds from abroad: higher-than-expected US inflation has strengthened bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike in December, which strengthens the dollar [7].

Key takeaway: the exchange rate is the barometer of confidence in Brazil's public finances. Since Lula's re-election in late October, the market has been waiting for a credible savings plan, and it judges this one too small to stabilize the debt [4][8].

The mechanism: if investors fear that public debt will spiral, they demand higher rates to lend to the state, or sell their reais for dollars. The currency falls, which makes imports more expensive and can reignite inflation [4][7].
External factors amplify the move: when US rates rise, money leaves emerging countries to be invested in dollars, and the real suffers twice over [7].
The vote on the bill's final points on Tuesday, November 17, and then in the Chamber, will show whether the plan can be strengthened or, on the contrary, watered down [3][5].

For you, a weak real makes Brazil cheaper if you travel there, and affects the prices of Brazilian products imported into Europe, such as coffee, orange juice or soybeans, which are paid for in dollars. French companies with a large presence in Brazil, such as Carrefour, see their local profits worth less in euros. No buy or sell advice here.

How it works: why a budget plan moves a currency

A country that spends more than it earns has to borrow. If investors doubt it will be able to repay, they demand higher rates or pull their money out, selling the local currency for dollars: the real falls [4]. A credible savings plan does the opposite, because it promises more stable debt. But the market looks at size and duration: 60 billion reais over a single year, or about 0.5% of GDP, is seen as too little by several fund managers, who want lasting spending rules [4]. There is also an external factor: when US rates rise, investing in dollars becomes more profitable, which weighs on all emerging-market currencies [7].
Precedents: the real under pressure
June 2, 2025
The dollar closes at 5.673 reais, its highest level before this Friday's [1].
It took about 17 months for the dollar to return to that level, under the combined effect of budget doubts and US interest rates [7].
October 26, 2026
The day after Lula's re-election, shares of state-owned Banco do Brasil lose up to 31% intraday, Bradesco 25%, and the stock exchange triggers a circuit breaker, an automatic trading halt [8].
State-linked stocks are the first to take the hit when the market fears for public finances [8].
November 6, 2026
The dollar ends at 5.511 reais, already its highest level of the year, after stronger-than-expected US jobs data [9].
A week later, it tops 5.65: pressure from US rates and budget doubts have added up [1][9].

news.2026-11-14-bahrein-iran-radar-ameri: Bahrain: Iran says it destroyed a US radar; Washington says it shot down two drones

On Friday, November 13, Iran's Revolutionary Guards claimed to have destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain, in retaliation for a strike on a telecommunications tower in southern Iran. The US military command denies this and says it shot down two drones [1][2][3].

According to the statement carried by state television, the strike responds to an “air aggression” against a telecommunications tower in Sirik County, in southern Iran; it does not specify the targeted base or the radar model [3][4].
US Central Command (Centcom) says it shot down the “two attack drones” launched toward Bahrain, without commenting on the Sirik strike [2][3]. AP was unable to verify the damage [3].
This is the first time since early September that Iran has claimed an attack on US military installations in a Gulf country [2].
Bahrain hosts the headquarters of the US Fifth Fleet in Manama [4].
Key takeaway: even without major bombing campaigns, the war continues through small strikes, and each incident in the Gulf can reignite escalation [1][2].

The Guards present the attack as a warning to Washington to stop its air operations and “oil smuggling” in the Strait of Hormuz, while Tehran makes any formal negotiations conditional on its demands [1][4].
What about me? A successful attack on the US Navy in the Gulf would quickly send oil prices back up, and with them the cost of filling up in France.

news.2026-11-14-malaisie-anwar-tensions-: Malaysia: Anwar plays down government tensions after his transport minister's resignation, on the eve of a test election in Malacca

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says the mood at the cabinet meeting on Friday, November 13, was “normal,” despite signs of tension in his coalition. He has not yet decided whether to accept the resignation of Transport Minister Loke, and says there is “no urgency” [1].
Anwar Ibrahim has not ruled on the resignation submitted by his transport minister, Loke, and says he does not want to rush [1].
The same day, he blamed government agencies for repeated flooding in the state of Selangor and ordered faster maintenance of canals and rivers, with more money and better coordination [2][3].
On Sunday, November 15, the state of Malacca goes to the polls. Anwar urged voters to reject those who exploit religion for political ends and the corrupt [4].
He will then lead the Malaysian delegation to the ASEAN summit in Manila, but will return early to host Emmanuel Macron on November 17 [5].
Key takeaway: the Malacca election serves as a test for Anwar's coalition, at a time when a government resignation is exposing its divisions [1][4].

An analyst interviewed by the Sarawak Tribune, however, considers it unlikely that Anwar will call early general elections: he would let Parliament serve out its full term, which ends late next year [6].
For you, Malaysia matters mainly as a supplier of electronic chips and palm oil. Emmanuel Macron's visit on November 17 will show whether Paris wants to strengthen its trade ties there.
